It keeps the color from muddying into brown or cooling down into a terracotta. It is bright, citrusy, and aggressive.

In #FF9300, the green value (93) is just high enough to keep it orange but low enough to avoid yellow. If you guessed a yellow-orange and the game told you "warmer," you needed more red. If it said "cooler," you needed less red or more yellow.

I personally guessed "debt" at #3, felt clever, then spun for ten minutes. That's the trap. Contexto punishes you for finding a strong semantic neighbor and assuming you're close in the ranking. You're not. "Debt" and "credit" are conceptually joined at the hip, but the model weights them differently depending on training context. I see this pattern about twice a week.

  • #5 LOAN — Keeps you in the financial lane, which is correct but narrow.
  • #11 BELIEF — This is where players derail. The algorithm is picking up "credit" as in "give credit," not just Visa and Mastercard.
  • #23 CARD — Too specific. "Credit card" is a phrase, but the model doesn't treat compounds kindly.

The #11 ranking for "belief" is the tell. I watched three people in a Discord thread ignore it because they were tunnel-visioned on banking. Contexto doesn't care about your category boxes. The vector for "credit" pulls from academic citations, movie credits, and personal reputation as much as it does from APR and FICO scores.

If your guesses are landing in the #40-#80 range and feeling "close but wrong," try abstracting. Ask what connects your guesses rather than what distinguishes them. That's usually the bridge.

When to guess vs when to think

There's a rhythm to Contexto that took me months to trust. Early guesses should be broad category probes. Middle game is where you map the semantic field. Late game is when you start playing word-association chicken with the algorithm.

Today, if you had "bank" at #7 and "money" at #12, the temptation is to drill down: "savings," "checking," "account." That's guessing. The better move is to lateral. What else sits near "bank" and "money" but isn't them? "Credit" is the obvious answer in hindsight, but "trust," "faith," and "reputation" all signal the same vector neighborhood.

I use a simple rule now: if three guesses in a row don't break into the top 5, I switch domains entirely. From finance to philosophy, or from objects to actions. The model's top clusters are usually narrower than your intuition suggests. Today's puzzle is a perfect case study—the answer sits at the intersection of two domains most players treat as separate.

Why does Contexto rank "credit" higher than "credibility" when they share a root?

The model doesn't parse morphology the way humans do. "Credit" as a noun has more training overlap with financial and social trust contexts. "Credibility" is more academic and rhetorical. The vectors diverge more than you'd expect. I've seen "credible" rank at #31 on a similar puzzle while "credit" sat at #1.

How does Contexto handle words with multiple meanings?

Poorly, from a human perspective. Brilliantly, from a distributional semantics perspective. "Credit" means both "academic unit" and "financial trust." The model averages these senses into a single vector. Your job is to guess the averaged point, not any individual meaning. That's why words like "trust" and "faith" rank high—they're also polysemous in overlapping ways.

Is there a faster way to solve when I'm stuck in the #20-#50 range?

Yes. Stop guessing synonyms and start guessing antonyms or functional equivalents. If "debt" is at #3 and you're stuck, try what debt enables or contrasts with. "Purchase," "spend," "borrow." Sometimes the model's path to your target runs through action verbs, not nouns. I cleared a #32 rut on Tuesday by switching from nouns to verbs entirely.

Why did my answer work yesterday but rank terribly today?

Because the target word changed. The model is static; the puzzle is daily. Your "instinct" for what Contexto likes is actually pattern-matching against past target distributions. Some days the answer is concrete ("hammer," #847 from March). Some days it's abstract like today. The archive helps you calibrate. I review it weekly to see if the editors are clustering around themes.

Does playing more Contexto actually improve your score?

Marginally, and then it plateaus. What improves is your tolerance for semantic noise. You stop expecting clean categories. You start seeing "close" as a directional hint, not a frustration. I'm not faster than I was at 200 puzzles, but I quit fewer games in anger. That counts for something.

worldle-answer-today.articleHtml:
The silhouette for May 26, 2026, is Slovakia. I burned two guesses on this one immediately because the northern border curve looks deceptively like a slice of Ukraine if you aren't paying attention to the western jagged edge. The shape is distinctively elongated east-to-west, but that northern dip is the tell. If you guessed a Balkan nation or something further south, the distance percentage likely threw you off, as Central Europe gets crowded fast.

Where in the world is today's answer?

Today's target sits right in the heart of Central Europe, landlocked and sandwiched between Poland to the north, Ukraine to the east, Hungary to the south, and Austria and the Czech Republic to the west. The shape is a bit of a stretched oval with a bite taken out of the top. It's easy to confuse this profile with Hungary, which lies directly south, but Hungary is wider and lacks that specific northern indentation. The key here is recognizing the cluster. When your first guess lands you within 500 kilometers but the direction points sharply north or south, you are likely oscillating within the same regional neighborhood. Check the Worldle archive to see how often these Central European shapes rotate into the daily slot; they appear more frequently than players expect because their distinct borders make for fair but tricky puzzles.

Reading the directional clues

The arrow behavior on this specific date was unforgiving for broad guesses. If you threw out "Europe" as a starter (which wastes a guess, by the way), the arrow pointed northwest. That narrows it down to the continent, sure, but it doesn't help with the specific country. The real data comes from the second and third guesses. I saw players in the comments panicking when a guess in Romania returned a "4%" distance match but an arrow pointing west. That 4% is misleadingly small; it implies proximity, but in Europe, 4% can still mean 300 kilometers. The percentage bar fills up faster in dense regions like the EU than it does for vast countries like Canada or Russia. Use the geography solver tool to cross-reference which countries fall within that shrinking radius. Don't just trust the percentage number; trust the arrow's consistency across three different guesses to triangulate the center point.

Mistakes that waste guesses

The biggest trap today was guessing Russia or Ukraine too early. Because the silhouette has that long eastern tail, eyes glaze over and assume "big eastern country." But the scale is off. Slovakia is compact. Guessing a massive neighbor skews your distance data because the game calculates from the geographic center of the country, not the border closest to your guess. If you guess Ukraine, the center is far to the east, giving you a massive distance error even if your border is technically close. Another common blunder was ignoring the landlocked status. Several top comments showed guesses like Croatia or even Sweden, ignoring the fact that today's shape has no coastline. Always verify if the shape touches water before guessing island nations or coastal states. Save your specific country guesses for when you have confirmed the region. Questions players keep asking

Why does the distance percentage change so drastically between guesses?

The percentage represents how much of the maximum possible distance you have covered relative to the game's internal scale, not a literal map measurement. In dense areas like Europe, a 1% change can mean moving 50 kilometers, whereas in South America, 1% might be 200 kilometers. The algorithm normalizes distance based on the size of the target country's bounding box. This is why guessing a neighbor often yields a low percentage like 2-5%, while a country on another continent shows 0%. It is a relative metric, not an absolute one. Focus on the trend: is the number going up? That is all that matters.

How do I distinguish between similar shapes like Hungary and Slovakia?

Look at the northern border. Slovakia's northern border with Poland is jagged and follows the Tatra Mountains, creating a distinct uneven line. Hungary's northern border is smoother and curves differently around Slovakia. Also, check the aspect ratio. Slovakia is wider than it is tall, whereas Hungary is slightly more square-like, though still rectangular. If you are stuck between the two, guess a country to the north of both, like Poland. The arrow will tell you instantly which one you are looking at. If the arrow points south, it is likely Slovakia; if it points southeast, you might be looking at Hungary. Generally, Worldle uses the standard recognized borders for the main contiguous landmass. Small exclaves usually do not appear in the silhouette unless they are significant in size. However, the game's database sometimes lags behind real-world geopolitical shifts or uses a specific dataset that might include or exclude certain border regions. If a shape looks "off" by a tiny sliver, do not let it throw your whole guess. Focus on the main body of the country. The core shape is what the game prioritizes for recognition.

Start with a large, centrally located country in the suspected continent to get a baseline distance and direction. For Europe, guessing France or Germany is often better than guessing a tiny nation like Luxembourg. Once you have a vector, move perpendicular to that line to triangulate. If you guess Germany and the arrow points East, you know you are looking at Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Austria, or Hungary. Your next guess should be one of those to cut the search space in half. Do not random guess small nations until you have eliminated the large ones that would skew your distance data.
